entries.name: scaling hypothesis
entries.senseHere: The view that intelligence comes from simple neural units and learning rules given enough data and computing power. Making networks bigger is the main route to human-level AI. DeepMind's 'weak' version says we also need to find the right algorithms piece by piece.

entries.name: GPT-3
entries.background: A very large language model released by OpenAI in 2020, with 175 billion adjustable numbers (parameters). It was trained only to predict the next word in huge amounts of Internet text.

entries.name: meta-learning
entries.senseHere: A model picking up a new task from just a few examples or a description in its prompt, without being retrained. GPT-3 was never built to do this.

entries.name: GPT-2
entries.background: OpenAI's 2019 language model, about 117 times smaller than GPT-3. It surprised people by writing fluent text.

entries.name: OpenAI
entries.background: The AI lab that built GPT-3. It began as a nonprofit and later added a for-profit arm to raise money for expensive computing.

entries.name: blessings of scale
entries.senseHere: The observation that making neural networks, data and computing bigger makes hard problems easier. Models become more stable, generalize better, and develop abilities like meta-learning.

entries.name: scaling laws
entries.background: Smooth, predictable patterns showing that a language model's error falls steadily as model size, data and computing grow. They let researchers forecast how much better a larger model will be.

entries.name: Transformer
entries.background: A neural network design from 2017 that lets each word in a text look at all the other words. It underlies GPT models.

entries.name: unsupervised learning
entries.background: Learning from raw data with no human-written labels. For GPT, the text itself supplies the answer: the next word.

entries.name: Hans Moravec
entries.background: Robotics researcher who predicted in the 1990s, from trends in computer power, when machines would match animals and then humans.

entries.name: connectionism
entries.background: The early approach to AI that builds intelligence from networks of simple artificial neurons, rather than hand-written rules.

entries.name: AGI
entries.background: Artificial general intelligence: AI that can handle a wide range of tasks as well as a human can.

entries.name: Jukebox
entries.background: An OpenAI model released in 2020 that generates raw audio music, including singing voices.

entries.name: pretraining thesis
entries.senseHere: The argument that training a model to predict text well forces it to learn logic, cause and effect, and common sense. Each remaining error needs a deeper kind of understanding to remove.

entries.name: Turing-NLG
entries.background: A 17-billion-parameter language model from Microsoft, the largest before GPT-3.

entries.name: AlphaGo Zero
entries.background: Game-playing AI systems from DeepMind. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero learned Go and chess by playing themselves, and AlphaStar played StarCraft.

entries.name: cross-entropy loss
entries.background: A score for how badly a model predicts the next character or word. Lower means better, and it can be counted in bits per character.

entries.name: neural nets are lazy
entries.senseHere: Networks first learn the easiest shortcuts, like memorizing or surface patterns. Only enough hard, varied data and training pushes them to learn the real underlying solution.

entries.name: DeepMind
entries.background: A London AI lab owned by Google. It built AlphaGo, AlphaZero and AlphaStar, and is known for drawing on brain science.

entries.name: Norbert Wiener
entries.background: American mathematician who founded cybernetics. In his 1950 book he argued that knowing a problem can be solved speeds up its solution.

entries.name: hardware overhang
entries.senseHere: The situation where enough computing power already exists for a breakthrough, but nobody has yet chosen to spend it that way.

entries.name: Ilya Sutskever
entries.background: A co-founder and chief scientist of OpenAI, and a long-time believer that big neural networks would work.

entries.name: Deep Blue
entries.background: IBM's chess computer that beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.

entries.name: intentional stance
entries.background: Philosopher Daniel Dennett's idea of explaining a system by treating it as an agent with goals. It works for people, and even for rivers 'wanting' to flow downhill.

entries.name: variational principle
entries.senseHere: Treating a physical system as 'wanting' to minimize one simple quantity, like a river lowering its height. You then predict its path without simulating every detail.

entries.name: agency
entries.senseHere: Not an all-or-nothing property but a continuum of ability to steer the world toward goals. A model trained on data from agents learns to imitate them and can act as one when prompted.

entries.name: SayCan
entries.background: A Google system that connects a language model to a real robot so it can turn spoken instructions into physical steps, like fetching a can.

entries.name: Janus
entries.background: A pseudonymous writer on language models who views GPT as a simulator of the world rather than as an agent.

entries.name: Conway's Game of Life
entries.background: A grid of cells that live or die by simple local rules. It produces moving patterns like 'gliders' and fixed ones called still lifes.

entries.name: Turing machine
entries.background: Alan Turing's abstract computer that follows rules to read and write symbols on an endless tape. The Busy Beaver is the program that runs longest before halting, for a given size.

entries.name: Occam's razor
entries.background: The principle that, of explanations fitting the facts equally well, the simpler one is preferred.

entries.name: Moore's law
entries.background: The observation that computer chips get roughly twice as powerful for the same cost every couple of years.
